extracted.intended_audience: policy analysts, regulatory economists, state agencies, advocacy organizations, and public commenters on the DHS proposed public charge rule
extracted.subtask_description: Economic and statutory analysis guidance used in the DHS notice-and-comment rulemaking to estimate changes in Federal and State transfer payments, indirect impacts, and statutory applicability for the proposed public charge rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction-in-transfer-payments estimation methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate reduction in transfer payments by multiplying a disenrollment/forgone enrollment rate by (1) the population of analysis (those who may disenroll or forgo enrollment) and (2) the value of the forgone benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with the 2019 and 2022 Final Rules, DHS applies this multiplicative approach across covered programs (Medicaid, CHIP, SNAP, TANF, SSI, Federal Rental Assistance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a range and primary estimate for disenrollment rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a lower bound, upper bound, and a primary (midpoint) estimate for the disenrollment/forgone enrollment rate rather than a single point estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS uses a low estimate (3.3%), an upper-bound estimate based on studies (17.3%), and a primary estimate of 10.3% (midpoint). DHS explains sources, acknowledges uncertainty, and welcomes public comment on the chosen rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low estimate derivation (3.3%) following prior methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Low estimate derived using the 2019/2022 methodology: dividing the annual number of approved aliens adjusting status by the estimated alien population and assuming 100% of such aliens and their household members are enrolled/eligible and would disenroll if concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS notes this assumption likely tends toward overestimation for the population directly regulated and uses it as a conservative low estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper-bound estimate based on empirical studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper estimate informed by multiple studies reporting reductions in enrollment (studies from 2016–2025 showing ranges such as 4.1% to 48%, and program-specific findings like 15%–35% disenrollment for Medicaid/CHIP in some analyses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS acknowledges heterogeneity across studies, program coverage (some studies excluded SSI/TANF), and methodological differences that could lead to over- or underestimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multi-year averages for program recipient counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a 6-year average of public benefit recipients' data (FY2019–FY2024) to estimate populations for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is done to remain consistent with averages used earlier in the economic analysis and to smooth year-to-year variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to estimate households with at least one alien
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate number of households receiving a benefit by dividing number of benefit recipients by U.S. average household size (2.54), then multiply estimated households by 6.61% (alien share of U.S. population) to get households with at least one alien, then multiply by foreign-born household size (3.12) to estimate number of aliens who received benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS acknowledges this introduces uncertainty because the percent of households with an alien may differ from the percent of aliens in the population; if aliens cluster in households, the method may overestimate households with at least one alien.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption that percent of aliens in population applies across public benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the U.S. Census Bureau's estimated alien population share (6.61%) holds across the populations of various public benefits programs to estimate households with at least one alien.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS explicitly notes this may introduce uncertainty because program-specific participation rates by aliens may vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average annual benefit per person estimation (program-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each program except Medicaid, compute average annual benefit per person by dividing average annual program payments by the average annual total number of recipients. For Medicaid, use CMS' median per capita expenditure across all States for calendar year 2022.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where data are available, use 6-year averages (FY2019–FY2024); Medicaid uses CMS median per-capita 2022 as most recent available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Medical Assistance Percentage (FMAP) usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an average FMAP of 59% across all States and U.S. territories to estimate combined Federal/State reductions in transfer payments for Medicaid and CHIP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS notes the 59% average may underestimate State participation because of previous enhanced FMAPs and invites comment on state contribution data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption of 100 percent Federal share for certain programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Conservatively assume the Federal Government pays 100% of benefits values for SNAP, TANF, and Federal Rental Assistance for the purposes of this analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS acknowledges State/local supplementation for some programs and states it cannot quantify State portions due to data limitations; it requests comments on State contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of costs over time using discount rates
rubrics_metrics.description: To compare costs over time, apply 3% and 7% discount rates and present undiscounted and discounted (3% and 7%) ten-year totals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS reports 10-year undiscounted and discounted estimates for Federal, State, and combined transfer payment reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of estimated reductions as transfers (not net resource losses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat estimated reductions in transfer payments as transfers (monetary payments from one group to another) that do not affect total resources available to society as a formal matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS emphasizes that transfers relate predominantly to enrollment decisions by those not subject to the public charge ground, and downstream effects are broader than direct disenrollment among regulated people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and inclusion of indirect impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider indirect impacts resulting from reduced transfer payments or behavioral changes, including familiarization costs, compliance costs, downstream public health effects, community stability, increased uncompensated care, economic effects on providers/retailers/agricultural producers/landlords, and administrative churn for states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS applies the same indirect impact analysis used in prior final rules and lists specific potential downstream consequences (worse health outcomes, higher communicable disease prevalence, increased uncompensated care, increased poverty/housing instability, reduced productivity and educational attainment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarization-cost estimation assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the time to read the rule as approximately 2 to 3 hours per person, assume an average professional reading rate of ~250–300 words per minute, and use an average total rate of compensation of $48.05 per hour to compute opportunity cost per reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From these assumptions, DHS estimates opportunity costs of about $96.10 to $144.15 per individual who reads the proposed rule. DHS cannot quantify the number of readers and requests comment on appropriate methodologies for quantifying readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and examples of regulatory compliance costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Define compliance costs broadly to include salaries of employees who monitor regulations, opportunity costs of time to understand requirements, dissemination and training costs, and IT system development or modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give examples of entities that may incur compliance costs (hospitals, state Medicaid agencies) and note data limitations in quantifying such burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of empirical evidence of chilling effects to inform estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate studies showing chilling effects (reduced enrollment due to immigration-policy fears) to inform upper-bound estimates and qualitative discussion of impacts across programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS cites multiple studies (KFF, Urban Institute, academic filings) reporting various magnitudes of disenrollment and acknowledges that studies differ in program coverage, populations, and methods, affecting reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with prior rule methodologies and recognition of biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain consistent methodologies with the 2019 and 2022 Final Rules (e.g., disenrollment-rate calculation), and explicitly acknowledge whether methodological choices are likely to over- or under-estimate effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS explains where methods may overestimate (assuming 100% enrolled/eligible) or underestimate (prior studies omitted some programs) and uses these considerations to frame low/primary/high estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) small-entity impact determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the proposed rule would have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, defining 'small entities' per RFA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS states the rule does not directly regulate small entities, individuals are not 'small entities' under RFA, and certifies there would not be a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities; indirect effects on entities are acknowledged but not treated as direct regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA) applicability test
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the rule contains a Federal mandate as defined under UMRA (i.e., imposes an enforceable duty resulting in aggregated expenditures exceeding the threshold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS concludes the proposed rule does not contain a UMRA Federal mandate because it imposes no enforceable duty on other levels of government or private entities; therefore Title II UMRA requirements do not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 13132 (Federalism) applicability test
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the proposed rule would have substantial direct effects on States, the relationship between national and State governments, or the distribution of power/responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS determines no sufficient federalism implications warranting a federalism summary impact statement under E.O. 13132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 12988 (Civil Justice Reform) drafting standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft and review the proposed rule to provide a clear legal standard for affected conduct and eliminate drafting errors and ambiguities to minimize litigation and undue burden on the Federal court system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS states the rule was written and reviewed per E.O. 12988 and meets applicable standards in section 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family Policymaking Assessment criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: When a rule may affect family well-being, assess seven criteria: (1) impacts on family stability/safety; (2) impacts on parental authority over education/nurture/supervision; (3) whether it helps the family perform functions; (4) effects on disposable income or poverty of families/children; (5) whether financial impacts are justified; (6) whether impact may be carried out by State/local government or family; (7) whether the rule establishes policy concerning youth behavior/personal responsibility norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS determines the rule may decrease disposable income and increase poverty for certain families (including U.S.-citizen children) but concludes benefits justify the financial impact and no further actions are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about quantification limits and requests for comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about data limitations and inability to quantify certain effects (downstream effects, State portions of payments, number of individuals who will familiarize themselves) and solicit public comments on appropriate methodologies and data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS repeatedly notes where it cannot quantify impacts, frames conservative assumptions where appropriate, and invites commenters to provide data and methodological suggestions to improve estimates.
